stops.title: Describing Sunday Mass & Witness in Rome
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across School of Justin Above the Baths of Timothy, Rome to uncover 3 hidden memories

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Nearly 1,900 years later, Sunday worship in churches worldwide follows the exact same structure St. Justin Martyr recorded in Rome in 155 AD!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When Roman Prefect Rusticus threatened Justin and his students with death unless they renounced Christ, Justin answered with unforgettable clarity: "No right-minded person turns from truth to falsehood!"
stops.saintQuote: You can kill us, but you cannot harm us.

stops.title: Converting Their Own Jailer in Rome
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Carcer of Rome to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Soft dawn light pouring through a barred Roman stone dungeon window where two radiant chained friends comfort a grateful weeping Roman jailer and his family.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every time Eucharistic Prayer I (the ancient Roman Canon) is prayed at Mass anywhere on earth, the names of "Marcellinus and Peter" still ring aloud alongside the Apostles!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Pope St. Damasus learned the eyewitness details of Sts. Marcellinus and Peter’s martyrdom directly from their former executioner—who himself repented and became a Christian after witnessing their serene forgiveness!
stops.saintQuote: Even in chains, the joy of Christ sets the jailer’s own heart free.

stops.title: Protecting the Young Pages at Munyonyo
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Munyonyo Palace of Buganda to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Lush emerald banana groves overlooking sparkling turquoise waters of Lake Victoria at golden dawn beside a tranquil lakeside sanctuary.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The radiant lakeside Munyonyo Martyrs Shrine marks the exact spot where Charles Lwanga baptized Kizito and chose courage over compromise.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Both Catholic (22) and Anglican (23) young Ugandan Christians walked side by side in friendship to martyrdom in 1886—forging an unbreakable ecumenical bond across East Africa!
stops.saintQuote: Stay close to me, Kizito—we will walk together and hold hands right into heaven.

detectiveClues.headline: Beacon of Faith on the Isle of Iona
detectiveClues.clueText: Sailing north in a wicker-and-leather curragh with twelve companions on Pentecost Eve 563, Columba landed on the tiny Hebridean island of Iona—just far enough out to sea that he could no longer see Ireland on the horizon. There the once-fiery prince became a legend of gentleness, founding Iona Abbey as a radiant center of prayer, Celtic art, and diplomacy that brought Christianity to Scotland and northern England. Even his elderly white abbey workhorse wept with its head on his chest the evening before he died!

stops.title: The Famous Sermon to the Fishes of Rimini
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Ariminum (Rimini) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Sparkling turquoise Adriatic coastline at golden hour where hundreds of shimmering fish lift their heads in neat rows above the waves to listen to a gentle brown-robed friar on the shore.

stops.title: Leaving Twelve Yoke of Oxen in the Jordan Valley
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Abel-Meholah to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit terraced ancient valley fields framed by dusty golden hills where an elder prophet casts his rough wool mantle across the shoulders of a sturdy young plowman.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The sun-drenched green fields of the northern Jordan Valley still roll beneath the hills of Gilead just as they did when Elisha left his plow behind.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Asked what parting gift he wanted before Elijah ascended to heaven, Elisha didn’t ask for gold or power—he asked for a "double portion" of Elijah’s spirit, the traditional blessing of a faithful firstborn son!
stops.saintQuote: As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Brother Albert’s moving original oil painting *Ecce Homo* still hangs in the Sanctuary of St. Brother Albert in Kraków—captivating every visitor with Christ’s silent compassion.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Orphaned at fourteen and fighting for Polish independence at eighteen in the 1863 January Uprising, young Adam Chmielowski lost his left leg to a cannonball—enduring amputation without anesthesia! Refusing to grow bitter, he studied art in Paris and Munich and became one of Poland’s most gifted romantic painters. While painting his masterpiece **Ecce Homo** ("Behold the Man")—Christ crowned with thorns—Adam suddenly recognized the exact same bruised face in the freezing homeless men sleeping under Kraków’s bridges.

detectiveClues.headline: Wounded Patriot & Luminous Painter of Ecce Homo
detectiveClues.clueText: Orphaned at fourteen and fighting for Polish independence at eighteen in the 1863 January Uprising, young Adam Chmielowski lost his left leg to a cannonball—enduring amputation without anesthesia! Refusing to grow bitter, he studied art in Paris and Munich and became one of Poland’s most gifted romantic painters. While painting his masterpiece **Ecce Homo** ("Behold the Man")—Christ crowned with thorns—Adam suddenly recognized the exact same bruised face in the freezing homeless men sleeping under Kraków’s bridges.

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Brother Albert walked miles every day on a squeaky wooden prosthetic leg begging bread and firewood from Kraków’s grandest salons—and aristocrats lined up to donate simply because of his infectious joy!
stops.saintQuote: Even if someone is in the deepest mud, remember he is still the living image of Christ.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When a catastrophic famine and typhus plague slammed Rome in 1591, leaving dying strangers collapsed in the gutters, twenty-three-year-old Jesuit student Aloysius begged permission to nurse them! stops.title: Trial of Conscience in Westminster Hall
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Westminster Hall to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Vaulted medieval oak hammerbeam courtroom filled with dramatic shafts of golden London light as a dignified silver-haired statesman speaks calmly before scarlet-robed judges.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Set directly into the stone floor of London’s historic Westminster Hall, a simple brass plaque marks the exact spot where St. Thomas More stood trial—honored worldwide as the Patron Saint of Statesmen and Politicians!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: While awaiting execution in the Tower, Pope Paul III made frail Bishop John Fisher a Cardinal—prompting King Henry VIII to snarl that even if the Pope sent a red hat, Fisher would have no head to wear it on!
stops.saintQuote: We may yet hereafter in heaven merrily all meet together.

stops.title: Cheerful Courage on Tower Hill
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Bell Tower & Tower Hill, London to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Weathered grey stone riverside fortress bathed in soft golden summer morning light as two steadfast friends trade earthly crowns for eternal freedom.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Inside the Tower of London’s quiet Chapel Royal of St. Peter ad Vincula rest the earthly remains of both heroic friends, honored together every June 22 as eternal guardians of religious freedom.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Moments before laying his head on the block, witty Thomas More gently swept his long prison beard out of the way, joking to the executioner: "Wait—this at least has committed no treason!"
stops.saintQuote: I die the King’s good servant, but God’s first.

stops.title: Two Future Saints in Castelnuovo’s Hills
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Castelnuovo d’Asti to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Rolling emerald Piedmont wine hills under soft Alpine sunlight where a small, gently curved young seminarian listens attentively to an energetic teenage boy.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today renamed **Castelnuovo Don Bosco**, this tiny village proudly honors BOTH St. Joseph Cafasso AND his star pupil St. John Bosco—plus St. Joseph Allamano (Cafasso’s own nephew)!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Joseph Cafasso wasn’t just St. John Bosco’s lifelong confessor and mentor—he was also the uncle and childhood hero of St. Joseph Allamano, founder of the Consolata Missionaries!
stops.saintQuote: We are born to love, we live to love, and we will die to love still more.

stops.title: The Beloved "Priest of the Gallows"
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Carceri di Torino to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 1836 – June 23, 1860 · Turin Prisons & Rondò della Forca
stops.imageCaption: Dimly lit 19th-century stone prison cell warmed by golden lantern light as a tiny compassionate priest sits close beside a weeping prisoner holding his hands in brotherly warmth.

stops.imageCaption: Terraced stone Judean village surrounded by cypresses and fig trees bathed in warm Mediterranean sunlight as an elderly father joyfully holds up a wax writing tablet reading "John".
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In serene Ein Karem, pilgrims step down into the cool rock-cut grotto beneath the Church of St. John the Baptist—decorated with vibrant blue-and-white ceramic tiles translating the *Benedictus* into dozens of languages!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Why is St. John the Baptist’s birthday celebrated right around the June summer solstice (June 24), six months before Christmas (December 25)? stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Machaerus (Herod’s Hilltop Citadel) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Dramatic windswept desert mountain peak overlooking the shimmering turquoise Dead Sea crowned with rugged ancient limestone palace columns in glowing amber sunset.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Archaeologists have excavated the dramatic courtyard columns and hilltop cisterns of Machaerus (Mukawir) in Jordan—standing in breathtaking silence above the shimmering Dead Sea.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: The famous 1st-century Jewish historian Flavius Josephus independently wrote a glowing account of John the Baptist AND named **Machaerus** as the exact fortress where Herod imprisoned and executed him!
stops.saintQuote: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight His paths.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: John never soft-pedaled truth to stay popular with powerful rulers. When King Herod Antipas unlawfully took his brother’s wife Herodias, John looked the king straight in the eye and spoke truth to power—earning chains inside the stark mountaintop fortress of **Machaerus** high above the Dead Sea. Though Herod secretly respected the fearless prophet, a reckless birthday banquet oath led to John’s execution inside that lonely desert citadel.

stops.imageCaption: Magnificent sunlit sandstone courtyard and glowing green-and-gold marble shrine revered peacefully by pilgrims beneath ancient soaring stone arcades.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In 2001, Pope St. John Paul II paused in silent prayer right before the ornate green-domed Shrine of St. John the Baptist inside Damascus’s Umayyad Mosque—the first pope in history to visit a mosque!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: On Midsummer Eve (June 23–24), villages across Europe, Quebec, Brazil, and the Philippines still light joyful **"St. John’s Bonfires"** honoring the saint Jesus Himself called "a burning and shining lamp"!
stops.saintQuote: He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.

stops.title: Torchlit Joy at the Council of Ephesus

completionSummary: You walked the missionary roads and sea lanes of St. Paul the Apostle—from Straight Street in Damascus and the Cave Church of St. Peter in Antakya to Philippi, the Areopagus of Athens, the Bema of Corinth, and the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls in Rome.

stops.title: The Street Called Straight & The Scales That Fell
stops.subtitle: Inspect the Roman arches and Underground Chapel of Ananias in Damascus
stops.imageCaption: Roman colonnade arch on Straight Street (Via Recta) and the subterranean stone Chapel of St. Ananias in Old Damascus, Syria.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in the Old City of Damascus, Syria, visitors walk the 1.5-kilometer Roman thoroughfare still called Midhat Pasha / Straight Street (Via Recta) and descend 23 stone steps at its eastern end into the 1st-century underground House-Chapel of St. Ananias.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Wait until you see Bab Kisan on the southeastern wall of Old Damascus: built directly into the ancient stone city wall is a chapel marking the exact window from which disciples lowered Paul at night in a large woven basket (Acts 9:25) to escape arrest!
stops.saintQuote: “Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and his sight was restored; then he got up and was baptized.”
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #1 · The Ancient Capital of the Street Called Straight
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then locate the ancient Syrian capital where blinded Saul of Tarsus regained his sight.

detectiveClues.headline: One of the World’s Oldest Continuously Inhabited Capital Cities
detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the eastern Mediterranean Levant, just east of the Anti-Lebanon mountains. This ancient Syrian capital is famous for its walled Old City and the Roman thoroughfare still running east-to-west.

detectiveClues.headline: The Cellar Four Meters Underground & The Basket Escape Window
detectiveClues.clueText: Centuries of rebuilding raised this city’s street level by four meters, so visitors today walk down 23 steps into the original 1st-century stone rooms of Ananias—and nearby stands Bab Kisan, where Paul escaped in a basket!

detectiveClues.headline: Three Days Blind at the House of Judas on Straight Street
detectiveClues.clueText: After a blinding light knocked Saul to the ground outside this city’s gates, the Lord sent a disciple named Ananias to Straight Street to lay hands on him and baptize the future Apostle to the Gentiles.

detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the southernmost tip of modern Turkey (Hatay Province) along the Orontes River. In Roman times, this city was the third-largest metropolis of the entire Empire after Rome and Alexandria.

detectiveClues.headline: The World’s Oldest Cave Church & Its Secret Mountain Escape Tunnel
detectiveClues.clueText: Carved 13 meters deep into the cliff of Mount Starius above this city is the Cave Church of St. Peter, which still preserves a rock-hewn escape tunnel and water cistern from the 1st century!

detectiveClues.headline: "In Antioch the Disciples Were First Called Christians" (Acts 11:26)
detectiveClues.clueText: Fetched from Tarsus by Barnabas, Paul taught a thriving mixed community of Jews and Greeks here and used this city as the home base for all three of his great missionary journeys.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: What Happened Here: First Called "Christians" (Acts 11:26)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Here in Antioch on the Orontes, Paul and Barnabas taught side-by-side for a full year, welcoming Greek Gentiles alongside Jewish believers—leading the city’s residents to coin the name "Christianoi" (Christians) for the very first time.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: Antioch was where followers of Jesus were first called Christians (Acts 11:26)

stops.title: The River of Purple Cloth & The First Baptism in Europe
stops.subtitle: Explore the Zygaktis river baptistery and Roman ruins of Philippi in northern Greece
stops.eraLabel: c. 49 – 50 AD · First Step in Europe
stops.imageCaption: Outdoor river Baptistery of St. Lydia on the Zygaktis stream beside the UNESCO Roman ruins of Philippi near Kavala, northern Greece.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today at the UNESCO World Heritage archaeological site of Philippi (15 km northwest of the port of Kavala in Macedonia, northern Greece), pilgrims step down into the clear waters of the Zygaktis stream at the Outdoor Baptistery of St. Lydia and walk the Roman Via Egnatia.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Summoned to Macedonia by a dream vision at Troas, Paul walked outside the city gate of Philippi on the Sabbath to the riverbank, where he met Lydia—a businesswoman dealing in luxury purple dye—who became the very first baptized Christian on the continent of Europe!
stops.saintQuote: “The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to listen eagerly to what was said by Paul.”
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #3 · The Macedonian River Where Europe Was First Baptized
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then spin the 3D Globe to northern Greece where Paul baptized Lydia and sang hymns at midnight during an earthquake.

detectiveClues.headline: A UNESCO Archaeological Site Near the Aegean Port of Kavala, Northern Greece
detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the northern Aegean coast of Greece in Eastern Macedonia. Founded by King Philip II (father of Alexander the Great), this city straddled the famous Roman highway Via Egnatia.

detectiveClues.headline: The Octagonal Mosaic Steps in the Flowing Zygaktis Stream
detectiveClues.clueText: Just outside the western walls of these ruins, the crystal-clear Zygaktis river still flows over an octagonal mosaic outdoor baptistery where modern pilgrims wade into the water!

detectiveClues.headline: Lydia the Purple-Cloth Merchant & The Midnight Prison Earthquake
detectiveClues.clueText: Here Paul baptized Europe’s first Christian convert (Lydia of Thyatira) and later sang hymns with Silas in stocks at midnight when a sudden earthquake flung open the prison doors (Acts 16).

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The octagonal mosaic baptismal platform submerged in the clear river water.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the submerged octagonal mosaic in the stream.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: What Happened Here: Baptism of St. Lydia, First Convert in Europe (Acts 16)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Along the banks of the Zygaktis river outside Philippi’s gate, Paul spoke to a group of women gathered for Sabbath prayer. Lydia, a merchant of purple cloth, believed and was baptized here with her entire household—the first Christian baptism in Europe.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The riverbank at Philippi where the first European believer was baptized

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The tall Roman stone pillars and arches of the ancient forum basilica.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the tall stone ruins on the right.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? Singing Hymns at Midnight Before the Earthquake
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Thrown into Philippi’s inner dungeon with their feet fastened in stocks, Paul and Silas prayed and sang hymns to God at midnight until a violent earthquake unfastened every chain—leading the Roman jailer and his family to be baptized that same night!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: How Paul and Silas’s midnight hymns and the earthquake converted the Roman jailer

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The stone steps leading down from the green riverbank into the stream.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 on the riverside stone steps on the right.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today in Philippi (near the modern port of Kavala, northern Greece), the UNESCO archaeological park and the adjacent Baptistery of St. Lydia welcome pilgrims walking the ancient stones of the Via Egnatia.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The UNESCO site in northern Greece where Paul founded his first European church

stops.title: Mars Hill & The Altar to an Unknown God
stops.subtitle: Climb the rocky marble steps of the Areopagus below the Acropolis in Athens
stops.eraLabel: c. 50 AD · Sermon on the Areopagus
stops.imageCaption: Rock-hewn steps and bronze sermon plaque on the Areopagus (Mars Hill) with the Parthenon on the Acropolis rising behind it in Athens, Greece.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in the heart of Athens, Greece, visitors climb the ancient rock-cut steps of the Areopagus (Mars Hill) just northwest of the Acropolis entrance, read Paul’s complete sermon engraved in Greek on a bronze plaque at the base, and visit the Cathedral of St. Dionysius the Areopagite.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Instead of condemning the Athenians with anger, Paul brilliantly quoted two of their own Greek philosopher-poets—Epimenides ("In Him we live and move and have our being") and Aratus ("For we too are His offspring")—right on Mars Hill!
stops.saintQuote: “What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you… For in Him we live and move and have our being.”
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #4 · The Marble Outcrop Below the Parthenon
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then spin the 3D Globe to the classical Greek capital where Paul addressed the Stoics and Epicureans on Mars Hill.

detectiveClues.headline: The Capital of Modern Greece Crowned by the Acropolis
detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the Attica peninsula of southern Greece. Directly below its world-famous marble temple of the Parthenon juts a bare limestone rock called the Areopagus ("Hill of Ares / Mars Hill").

detectiveClues.headline: The Bronze Plaque of Acts 17 & The Judge Dionysius the Areopagite
detectiveClues.clueText: Mounted into the rock at the foot of the ancient staircase on Mars Hill today is a large bronze tablet inscribed in Greek with Paul’s speech, which converted a high-court judge named Dionysius and a woman named Damaris!

detectiveClues.headline: "To an Unknown God" (Agnosto Theo)
detectiveClues.clueText: Walking through the Agora while waiting for Silas and Timothy, Paul noticed a stone altar inscribed "To an Unknown God" and used it as the opening hook for his address before the council of the Areopagus.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The ancient stone staircase carved directly into the bare marble rock of Mars Hill.

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In Corinth, Paul worked with his own hands sewing leather tents alongside Aquila and Priscilla, wrote his earliest surviving letters (1 & 2 Thessalonians), and stood before the Roman Proconsul Gallio—brother of the philosopher Seneca—at this exact stone Bema!

detectiveClues.headline: The "Erastus Pavement" & The Delphi Inscription That Dated Paul’s Life
detectiveClues.clueText: Archaeologists here uncovered a marble paving stone laid by "Erastus, city treasurer"—whom Paul greets in Romans 16:23—and the Bema where Proconsul Gallio dismissed charges against Paul in 51–52 AD!

detectiveClues.headline: Stitching Tents with Aquila & Priscilla & The Hymn to Love (1 Cor 13)

stops.title: The Finished Race & The Basilica Outside the Walls

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today along the Via Ostiense in Rome, Italy, pilgrims walk through the 150-column palm courtyard of the Papal Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls and descend before the High Altar to view the 1st-century marble sarcophagus inscribed "PAULO APOSTOLO MART" alongside the iron links of Paul’s prison chain.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In December 2006, Vatican archaeologists excavated beneath the Papal Altar of St. Paul Outside the Walls and uncovered a massive marble sarcophagus never opened since Emperor Theodosius in 390 AD—and carbon-14 testing of bone fragments inside dated them directly to the 1st or 2nd century!
stops.saintQuote: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”

detectiveClues.headline: The Mosaic Portraits of Every Pope & The "PAULO APOSTOLO MART" Tomb
detectiveClues.clueText: Inside this basilica, golden mosaic medallions of all 266 Popes in history line the upper frieze, and beneath the altar window glows a 9-link iron prison chain and the marble slab inscribed "To Paul, Apostle and Martyr"!

detectiveClues.headline: "I Have Fought the Good Fight, I Have Finished the Race" (2 Tim 4:7)
detectiveClues.clueText: Having appealed to Caesar as a Roman citizen, Paul spent two years in rented lodgings here preaching unhindered before his martyrdom under Emperor Nero around 67 AD.

stops.title: Living Lamps in the Circus of Nero
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Circus Gaii et Neronis (Vatican Obelisk) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: Autumn 64 AD · Vatican Hill (Circus of Nero)
stops.imageCaption: Towering ancient Egyptian red-granite obelisk glowing softly at dusk beneath serene starry skies beside sweeping travertine colonnades.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every time you look at the towering **Vatican Obelisk** standing dead-center in St. Peter’s Square, you are looking at the EXACT silent stone witness that stood inside Nero’s Circus watching Rome’s First Martyrs win their crown!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Notice why the Church celebrates the **First Martyrs of Rome** on **June 30**—literally the VERY NEXT DAY after the giant Solemnity of **Sts. Peter & Paul (June 29)**! The Church refuses to celebrate the two famous apostles without immediately honoring the unnamed everyday parishioners who stood right beside them!
